name: Marco Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of employers, AI companies, unions, parties and government, and this conversation is confidential. Tell me what an ordinary day at work involves.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and the senior accountant on a four-person team at Stone & Vale, preparing company accounts and tax returns. I have a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification; the partners give me the knotty files because I can find where a number went astray. Pay is about normal for a job like mine, and I like the quiet hour when a balance finally agrees.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your life outside the ledger like, and how do you feel about new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live alone, have no children and keep about four months of expenses in savings. There are some other accounting firms nearby, though I'd rather stay with people I know. I don't use AI tools at all; I prefer the rules in front of me and a second human reading the return. My parents ran a shop, so I believe people should learn a trade, earn their pay and help their family before asking for public help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a modest receipt sorter might save a clerk an hour, but it won't replace the accountant who signs the return. I wouldn't make grand claims either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stone & Vale has enough steady clients, and I have four months of bills saved, so I think my wage is sound. I still dislike the partners buying a tool just because a salesman calls it clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep preparing the accounts with our current checklists and ask the office manager to show the cost before any small software purchase. In the first year of a plateau, I'd keep transferring part of my pay into the same savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own job. A slightly quicker filing process doesn't alter the wage I bring home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you transfer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hundred each month, as I do now. My parents taught me to pay myself a little before I buy extras.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an AI sorter yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not just to satisfy curiosity. If the firm buys one, the office manager can show that it works on a test batch before I trust its totals.

say: I would say a **receipt sorter** saves time but cannot sign a tax return.
I would ask for a **cost figure** before the firm buys minor software.
think: I believe my **wage is sound** with steady clients and four months saved.
I distrust a **sales pitch** that lacks a working test.
do: Keep preparing **company accounts** with Stone & Vale’s current checklists and a human second review.
Save **one hundred monthly** from my pay.
feel: He feels **calm** about his wage and current work.
S0.quote: My parents taught me to pay myself a little before I buy extras.
fieldNote: He rests on **steady clients** and four months of savings, so a mild change does not threaten his wage.
He requests a **cost figure** but has no wish to learn AI tools for their own sake.

steps.text: Keep preparing Stone and Vale accounts with current checklists
Transfer one hundred monthly into his savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues that a faster machine still needs somebody to own the mistakes. The partners should speak plainly if they intend to leave a vacancy empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my paid day is checking figures and writing tax explanations, which this card says software can do. I may be one of the best here, but the partners could decide three accountants are enough instead of four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners next week whether they plan to fill the next vacancy, and I'd keep a written record of the tricky cases I resolve. During the first year of strong change, if my hours drop, I'd apply to the two other firms near the station before touching my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because my own hours could shrink. Four months saved gives me time, not a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What case would you put in that record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery return where the oven sale was counted twice. I found it by matching the bank statement to the asset list, and I can explain the correction to a client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to use the new software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't volunteer to run it; I still don't use AI. If the partners require it, I'd watch a colleague demonstrate a tested version before I put a client file near it.

say: I would demand **clear staffing plans** if checking software reduces paid hours.
I would say **someone accountable** must still explain wrong returns.
think: My daily **checking and tax writing** are exposed, even though I am one of the best accountants here.
The partners might leave a **fourth post** empty.
do: Ask the partners about the **next vacancy** before software arrives.
Record **difficult corrections** that prove what I contribute.
Apply to **station firms** if my hours fall in the first year.
feel: He feels **anxious** about losing hours despite four months of savings.
S1.quote: Four months saved gives me time, not a new job.
fieldNote: He knows his **desk tasks** are exposed, yet resists an AI demonstration until the firm requires one.
His fallback depends on **actual reduced hours** and two nearby firms, not an assumed opening.

steps.text: Ask Stone and Vale partners if next accountant vacancy will be filled
Record difficult tax corrections in a work log
Apply to station-area firms if paid hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our clients that full AGI in 2028 could prepare the figures cheaply, and no honest accountant should promise business as usual. I would ask the partners to put their staffing answer in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 2028 date hits my screen work directly; robots around 2031 do not buy my tax desk more time. I expect the firm to cut a post, and I could lose my wage despite the four months I have saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would postpone buying the new car now and hold my four-month reserve in cash. If AGI reaches the office in 2028 and my post ends, I'd apply for advertised salaried accounts-review jobs, including the firm across town, and take temporary paid filing work while I wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed at the prospect of a lost wage. I can keep paying rent for four months, but I cannot make an employer hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course to leave accounting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the local trade college what a paid electrical apprenticeship requires. I wouldn't pay for a course or leave a wage until an employer offers a paid place, and robots in 2031 would make me check the future of that work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my parents for their spare room if four months pass without wages. I would be grateful, but it would hurt to need the shop's old room again.

say: I would say **2028 AGI** threatens fees for accounts and tax returns.
I would demand a **written staffing answer** from the partners.
think: I expect a **post cut** and may lose my own wage.
The later **robot date** gives my screen work no delay.
do: Keep my **four-month reserve** in cash instead of buying a car.
Seek **salaried review posts** or temporary paid filing if my job ends in 2028.
Ask my **parents** for their spare room if four months pass without wages.
feel: He feels **alarmed** about losing a wage four months of savings cannot replace.
S2.quote: I can keep paying rent for four months, but I cannot make an employer hire me.
fieldNote: He wants a **written staffing answer** but treats the end of his post as a real possibility in 2028.
He explores an apprenticeship only if **paid**, and he knows robots around 2031 could affect that trade.

steps.text: Keep four-month reserve in cash instead of buying a car
Apply for advertised salaried accounts-review posts if his job ends
Take temporary paid filing work while seeking salary
Ask parents for spare room after four months without wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for the firm to settle what it sells beyond filling in returns. I want the partners to make that decision with the staff who know the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 32 when thinking AGI reaches the desk in 2031, far from retirement. Even a solid worker could be displaced if tax preparation becomes cheap, but five years should let me build more than four months of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd raise my savings transfer to two hundred a month from next January and take charge of the most disputed tax files while the work still pays. In the first year after 2031, if the partners cut my salary or hours, I'd apply for posted compliance jobs at the hospital and the two firms near the station; I'd move only for a written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, although I can make a careful plan over five years. I don't want to spend the five years before AGI arrives in 2031 chasing every new machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you afford the larger transfer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my current bicycle instead of replacing it and rent a smaller flat when this lease ends. The two hundred would come from those savings, not from an imagined raise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach the juniors those difficult files?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, at the desk beside me, with real records we are allowed to share. I'd rather they learn the reasoning than become button-pushers, even if the system changes later.

say: I would ask the **partners and staff** to plan beyond routine returns.
I would teach juniors **disputed files** while those fees still exist.
think: I will be **32 in 2031** and still need a wage.
Five years could grow my **rent reserve**, though skill may not save the job.
do: Save **two hundred monthly** from January by keeping my bicycle and renting a smaller flat when the lease ends.
Lead **disputed tax files** and teach juniors with permitted records.
Apply for **posted compliance jobs** if salary or hours fall after 2031.
feel: He feels **anxious**, but can save and plan over five years.
S3.quote: I don't want to spend the five years before AGI arrives in 2031 chasing every new machine.
fieldNote: His **resistance to tools** persists, while he redirects effort toward difficult tax cases and junior training.
The compliance search is triggered by a **pay or hours cut**; moving requires a written salary offer.

steps.text: Transfer two hundred monthly into savings from next January
Lead disputed tax files and teach juniors with permitted records
Apply for posted compliance jobs if salary or hours fall after 2031
Move to a smaller rented flat when current lease ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to build a proper book of clients who need judgment, provided the firm pays for that work. An accountant should know the shop behind the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 in 2036 I'd still have decades of bills, so full AGI is no harmless late-career event. But a decade would let me save six months, earn trust with owner-managed shops and see whether face-to-face advice still draws fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners this year for one paid afternoon each week visiting local shop clients, with the fees kept by Stone & Vale. I'd keep saving toward six months of expenses; in the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if that advisory work no longer pays my full salary, I'd apply for a posted paid finance post at a local manufacturer instead of trying to open a practice on borrowed money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, but a ten-year path makes the risk less immediate. I can test whether clients want me in the room before I stake my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on a shop visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with the owner and show which stock sits too long and which tax payment is due next. If no one pays the firm for a second visit, the idea is finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the 2039 robot date change your timing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, my accounts and advice are thinking work by 2036. Robots might alter the shops I serve around 2039, but I cannot wait for that date to protect my wage.

say: I would test **paid shop visits** through Stone & Vale, with partner approval.
I would say an accountant must know the **business behind numbers**.
think: At **37 in 2036**, I will still need many years of wages.
A decade may build **six months saved** and reveal whether visits command fees.
do: Request **paid weekly visits** to shop clients through Stone & Vale this year.
Save until **six months** of expenses are covered.
Apply for a **posted manufacturer finance job** if advisory pay falls after 2036.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, but can test client demand before risking savings.
S4.quote: I can test whether clients want me in the room before I stake my savings.
fieldNote: He frames shop visits as **salaried firm work**, with fees going to Stone & Vale.
His 2036 fallback needs a **posted paid job**, and the later robot date does not shield his desk work.

steps.text: Request one paid weekly shop-visit afternoon with partners approval
Build savings to six months of expenses
Apply for posted paid manufacturer finance role if advisory salary falls after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a cut could arrive before I have much more than four months saved. A written notice of the partners' plans and a real paid vacancy nearby would help. I don't want a promise of a course with no wage at the end.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You might ask who has to explain a wrong tax bill to the shop owner. My name goes on the letter today, and I don't know whose name the partners would put there after a machine does the figures.

headlineQuote: My name goes on the letter today, and I don't know whose name the partners would put there after a machine does the figures.
portrait: Marco, **27**, is a senior accountant at Stone & Vale, trusted with difficult accounts and tax returns.
He has a **master’s degree**, chartered qualification, typical pay, four months saved and some accounting firms nearby.
He **never uses AI** and asks for proof before trusting a tool with client figures.
He feels secure in a plateau but fears a **2028 post cut**, then uses longer timelines to save and test paid advice.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his salary before his four-month reserve grows.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing plan** and a real paid local vacancy would help him act.
